checks: Fresh independent practice attempts start with zero credit, ready manual addressing and local gateways, disabled router IPv6 forwarding, and no router static routes or dynamic protocols.
Both published IOS configuration sets and the completed reference earn four configuration goals; six real IPv4/IPv6 echo tests are required to earn all ten tasks.
R1 has only IPv4 and IPv6 defaults. The same defaults reach both the upstream server LAN and loopback; packet events prove the selected upstream egress.
ip default-gateway does not install a routed IPv4 default or enable transit forwarding while IPv4 routing is enabled.
Removing either R1 default breaks both remote networks only in that address family; local connected gateway access and the other family remain operational.
Each missing upstream return route prevents replies despite the correct R1 default and requests being forwarded onto the server LAN; restoration repairs real traffic.
Disabling IPv6 forwarding on either router prevents IPv6 transit without affecting IPv4.
Uplink shutdown withdraws both defaults and upstream return routes, while connected branch gateway access continues. Restoring the uplink rebuilds routes and neighbors.
Connected branch LAN prefixes take precedence over defaults on the actual return-packet egress.
Unknown IPv4 and IPv6 destinations stop at ISP1; no reciprocal defaults create a forwarding loop.
A more-specific route, wrong default distance or incorrectly scoped IPv6 next hop cannot earn the intended default configuration task.

All published verification commands execute, including route lookup, Neighbor Discovery verification, route print, ping and traceroute. IPv4 output shows S* and a gateway of last resort; IPv6 shows S ::/0 and its scoped next hop.
Portable YAML save/reload and startup power cycles retain manual endpoint gateways, route configuration and previously earned traffic while active tables rebuild.
